1.o: We have here, I. God's kindness to Israel, in multiplying them exceedingly, (ver. 1-7). II. The Egyptians' wickedness to them, 1. Oppressing and enslaving them, (ver. 8-14). 2. Murdering their children, (ver. 15-22). Thus whom the court of heaven blessed the country of Egypt cursed, and for that reason.
1.i: A new king forgets Joseph and forces the growing Israelites into hard labor building cities.
1.p: Lord, You see the oppressed and You do not forget them. Help us to remember and to help. Amen.
1.l: Do something kind today for someone who works hard, like a parent, a cook, or a helper.
q: The Egyptians forgot what Joseph had done. Whose kindness have you forgotten?

2.o: This chapter begins the story of Moses, that man of renown, famed for his intimate acquaintance with Heaven and his eminent usefulness on earth, and the most remarkable type of Christ, as a prophet, saviour, lawgiver, and mediator, in all the Old Testament.
2.i: Moses' mother hides him in a basket in the Nile, and Pharaoh's daughter finds him and raises him as her son.
2.p: Lord, You keep Your children safe in ways we never plan. Thank You for the quiet courage of mothers and sisters. Amen.
2.l: Thank someone who cared for you when you were small, a parent, a grandparent, or a teacher.
q: The danger and the rescue came from the same Pharaoh's house. How has God used an unexpected person in your life?

3.o: As prophecy had ceased for many ages before the coming of Christ, that the revival and perfection of it in that great prophet might be the more remarkable, so vision had ceased (for aught that appears) among the patriarchs for some ages before the coming of Moses, that God's appearances to him for Israel's salvation might be the more welcome; and in this chapter we have God's first appearance to him in the bush and the conference between God and Moses in that vision. Here is, I.
3.s: The Bush That Did Not Burn Up
3.i: Moses sees a bush that burns without burning up, and God calls him to lead Israel out of Egypt.
3.p: Lord, You are the God who is. Be with us wherever You send us. Amen.
3.l: Take off your shoes for a moment today, stand quietly, and tell God that you know He is with you.
q: God did not say who Moses was but who He is. What does it mean that God is I AM?

4.o: This chapter, I. Continues and concludes God's discourse with Moses at the bush concerning this great affair of bringing Israel out of Egypt. 1. Moses objects the people's unbelief (ver. 1), and God answers that objection by giving him a power to work miracles, (1.) To turn his rod into a serpent, and then into a rod again, ver. 2-5. (2.) To make his hand leprous, and then whole again, ver. 6-8. (3.) To turn the water into blood, ver. 9. 2. Moses objects his own slowness of speech (ver.
4.i: God turns Moses' shepherd's staff into a snake and back, as a sign to show Israel that He has sent him.
4.p: Lord, take what is in our hands and use it for Your glory. Amen.
4.l: Look around today and ask God how He might use something small that you already have.
q: God asked Moses what was in his hand. What do you have that He could use?

5.o: Moses and Aaron are here dealing with Pharaoh, to get leave of him to go and worship in the wilderness. I. They demand leave in the name of God (ver. 1), and he answers their demand with a defiance of God, ver. 2. II. They beg leave in the name of Israel (ver. 3), and he answers their request with further orders to oppress Israel, ver. 4-9. These cruel orders were, 1. Executed by the task-masters, ver. 10-14. 2. Complained of to Pharaoh, but in vain, ver. 15-19. 3. Complained of by the people to Moses ver.
5.i: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh to let Israel go, and Pharaoh makes the work harder by taking away the straw.
5.p: Lord, when things get worse before they get better, help us to keep trusting You. Amen.
5.l: Be patient today with someone who is going through a hard time, and do not expect things to get better right away.
q: Things got worse before they got better for Israel. Where are you in the middle of a hard stretch?

6.o: Much ado there was to bring Moses to his work, and when the ice was broken, some difficulty having occurred in carrying it on, there was no less ado to put him forward in it. Witness this chapter, in which, I. God satisfies Moses himself in an answer to his complaints in the close of the foregoing chapter, ver. 1. II. He gives him fuller instructions than had yet been given him what to say to the children of Israel, for their satisfaction (ver. 2-8), but to little purpose, ver. 9. III.
6.i: Exodus 6 gives God's answer to Moses' discouragement: a name, a set of promises, and a plan that does not depend on how the people feel.
6.p: Lord, You are the LORD, who hears groaning and keeps promises. Help us to trust You when we are too tired to feel hope. Amen.
6.l: When life is hard today, say one of God's promises out loud, even if you do not feel it.
q: The people were too discouraged to hear good news. What promise of God do you most need to hear today?

7.o: In this chapter, I. The dispute between God and Moses finishes, and Moses applies himself to the execution of his commission, in obedience to God's command, ver. 1-7. II. The dispute between Moses and Pharaoh begins, and a famous trial of skill it was. Moses, in God's name, demands Israel's release; Pharaoh denies it. The contest is between the power of the great God and the power of a proud prince; and it will be found, in the issue, that when God judgeth he will overcome. 1.
7.i: God turns the Nile to blood as the first plague on Egypt.
7.p: Lord, You are the source of all life. Teach us to depend on You, and not only on the gifts You give. Amen.
7.l: Say thank you today for clean water, every time you take a drink.
q: The Egyptians trusted the Nile completely. What do you trust in that could be taken away?

8.o: Three more of the plagues of Egypt are related in this chapter, I. That of the frogs, which is, 1. Threatened, ver. 1-4. 2. Inflicted, ver. 5, 6. 3. Mimicked by the magicians, ver. 7. 4. Removed, at the humble request of Pharaoh (ver. 8-14), who yet hardens his heart, and, notwithstanding his promise while the plague was upon him (ver. 8), refuses to let Israel go, ver. 15. II. The plague of lice (ver. 16, 17), by which, 1. The magicians were baffled (ver. 18, 19), and yet, 2. Pharaoh was hardened, ver. 19. III.
8.i: God sends a plague of frogs on Egypt, and Pharaoh promises to let Israel go and then changes his mind.
8.p: Lord, give us honest hearts that keep promises, even when the trouble has passed. Amen.
8.l: When you say you will do something because you are in trouble, remember to follow through when the trouble is over.
q: Pharaoh changed his mind as soon as the trouble stopped. Do you ever do that?

9.o: In this chapter we have an account of three more of the plagues of Egypt. I. Murrain among the cattle, which was fatal to them, ver. 1-7. II. Boils upon man and beast, ver. 8-12. III. Hail, with thunder and lightning. 1. Warning is given of this plague, ver. 13-21. 2. It is inflicted, to their great terror, ver. 22-26. 3. Pharaoh, in a fright, renews his treaty with Moses, but instantly breaks his word, ver. 27, &c.
9.s: Hail on Egypt, Light in Goshen
9.i: God sends hail on Egypt but spares Goshen, and those who heed His warning bring their animals in.
9.p: Lord, You warn us because You care. Give us ears to hear and hearts to obey. Amen.
9.l: When someone gives you good advice today, listen to it the first time.
q: Some Egyptians listened to God's warning and were saved. What warnings are you tempted to ignore?

10.o: The eighth and ninth of the plagues of Egypt, that of locusts and that of darkness, are recorded in this chapter. I. Concerning the plague of locusts, 1. God instructs Moses in the meaning of these amazing dispensations of his providence, ver. 1, 2. 2. He threatens the locusts, ver. 3-6. 3. Pharaoh, at the persuasion of his servants, is willing to treat again with Moses (ver. 7-9), but they cannot agree, ver. 10, 11. 4. The locusts come, ver. 12-15. 5. Pharaoh cries Peccavi—I have offended (ver.
10.i: A swarm of locusts covers Egypt and eats everything the hail left, and Pharaoh again refuses to let Israel go.
10.p: Lord, You are in charge of wind and wave and swarm. Soften our hearts when You speak to us. Amen.
10.l: Pick one thing today you will not take for granted, like a meal, and thank God for it.
q: Pharaoh wanted the plague gone but not the cause. When do you wish for the results to go away without a change of heart?

11.o: Pharaoh had told Moses to get out of his presence (ch. x. 28), and Moses had promised this should be the last time he would trouble him, yet he resolves to say out what he had to say, before he left him; accordingly, we have in this chapter, I. The instructions God had given to Moses, which he was now to pursue (ver. 1, 2), together with the interest Israel and Moses had in the esteem of the Egyptians, ver. 3. II. The last message Moses delivered to Pharaoh, concerning the death of the firstborn, ver. 4-8. III.
11.i: Exodus 11 is the warning before the last of the ten plagues, and a chapter that shows the same Moses who was afraid at the burning bush, now standing in front of the king.
11.p: Lord, You are patient and You are just. Keep us from hardening our hearts when You speak to us. Amen.
11.l: Pray today for people who are in a place of sorrow, and ask God to comfort them.
q: God would not let Israel leave without their wages. Who is owed something from you, even if they have stopped asking?

12.o: This chapter gives an account of one of the most memorable ordinances, and one of the most memorable providences, of all that are recorded in the Old Testament. I. Not one of all the ordinances of the Jewish church was more eminent than that of the passover, nor is any one more frequently mentioned in the New Testament; and we have here an account of the institution to it. The ordinance consisted of three parts:—1. The killing and eating of the paschal lamb, ver. 1-6, 8-11. 2.
12.i: God tells Israel to take a lamb, put its blood on their doorframes, and eat in haste, the first Passover.
12.p: Lord, You passed over us in mercy. Teach us to remember what You have done and to tell our children. Amen.
12.l: Ask a grown-up to tell you the story of Passover, and tell it to someone else.
q: The blood on the door was a sign of trust. What shows others that you trust God?

13.o: In this chapter we have, I. The commands God gave to Israel, 1. To sanctify all their firstborn to him, ver. 1, 2. 2. To be sure to remember their deliverance out of Egypt (v. 3, 4), and, in remembrance of it, to keep the feast of unleavened bread, ver. 5-7. 3. To transmit the knowledge of it with all possible care to their children, ver. 8-10. 4. To set apart unto God the firstlings of their cattle, (ver. 11-13), and to explain that also to their children, ver. 14-16. II.
13.s: A Pillar by Day and by Night
13.i: God leads Israel the long way around, in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night, with Joseph's bones in their midst.
13.p: Lord, You go before us day and night. Lead us in the way we should go. Amen.
13.l: The next time you are not sure what to do, say a prayer, and wait to see how God shows you.
q: God did not take the nearest road because the people were not ready. What delay in your life might be about readiness?

14.o: The departure of the children of Israel out of Egypt (which was indeed the birth of the Jewish church) is made yet more memorable by further works of wonder, which were wrought immediately upon it. Witness the records of this chapter, the contents whereof, together with a key to it, we have, Heb. xi. 29. "They passed through the Red Sea as by dry land, which the Egyptians assaying to do were drowned;" and this they did by faith, which intimates that there was something typical and spiritual in it. Here is, I.
14.i: Israel is camped at the sea when Pharaoh's army charges, and Moses tells them to stand still and see the Lord's salvation.
14.p: Lord, when we feel trapped, remind us that You fight for us. Help us to be still and trust You. Amen.
14.l: The next time you feel trapped, take a deep breath and say, The Lord will fight for me.
q: Israel grumbled when they were frightened. What do you say when you are afraid?

15.o: In this chapter, I. Israel looks back upon Egypt with a song of praise for their deliverance. Here is, 1. The song itself, ver. 1-19. 2. The solemn singing of it, ver. 20, 21. II. Israel marches forward in the wilderness (ver. 22), and there, 1. Their discontent at the waters of Marah (ver. 23, 24), and the relief granted them, ver. 25, 26. 2. Their satisfaction in the waters of Elim, ver. 27.
15.i: After crossing the sea, Moses and Israel sing to the Lord, and Miriam leads the women in dance with tambourines.
15.p: Lord, You are our strength and our song. We praise You for saving us. Amen.
15.l: Sing a song of thanks to God today, loudly, with a friend or alone.
q: Israel sang when they were safe. What songs do you sing to remember what God has done?

16.o: This chapter gives us an account of the victualling of the camp of Israel. I. Their complaint for want of bread, ver. 1-3. II. The notice God gave them beforehand of the provision he intended to make for them, ver. 4-12. III. The sending of the manna, ver. 13-15. IV. The laws and orders concerning the manna. 1. That they should gather it daily for their daily bread, ver. 16-21. 2. That they should gather a double portion on the sixth day, ver. 22-26. 3. That they should expect none on the seventh day, ver. 27-31.
16.i: Israel grumbles about food in the desert, and God sends quail in the evening and manna each morning.
16.p: Lord, give us this day our daily bread. Thank You for providing for Your people. Amen.
16.l: Say thank you for your food before the next meal, and think of how God feeds His people.
q: The manna was never mistaken for a product of nature. What daily provision do you treat as natural that is in fact given?

17.o: Two passages of story are recorded in this chapter, I. The watering of the host of Israel. 1. In the wilderness they wanted water, ver. 1. 2. In their want they chided Moses, ver. 2, 3. 3. Moses cried to God, ver. 4. 4. God ordered him to smite the rock, and fetch water out of that; Moses did so, ver. 5, 6. 5. The place named from it, ver. 7. II. The defeating of the host of Amalek. 1. The victory obtained by the prayer of Moses, ver. 8-12. 2. By the sword of Joshua, ver. 13. 3. A record kept of it, ver. 14, 16.
17.i: At Rephidim, with no water, Israel quarrels with Moses, and God brings water from the rock at Horeb.
17.p: Lord, You give water from rocks. Forgive our complaining and give us trust. Amen.
17.l: Before you complain today, pause and ask God for what you need instead.
q: Israel asked, Is the Lord among us or not? When have you asked that question?

18.o: This chapter is concerning Moses himself, and the affairs of his own family. I. Jethro his father-in-law brings to him his wife and children, ver. 1-6. II. Moses entertains his father-in-law with great respect (ver. 7), with good discourse (ver. 8-11), with a sacrifice and a feast, ver. 12. III. Jethro advises him about the management of his business as a judge in Israel, to take inferior judges in to his assistance (ver. 13-23), and Moses, after some time, takes his counsel (ver. 24-26), and so they part, ver. 27.
18.i: Jethro visits Moses, sees him judging alone, and advises him to choose leaders to share the work.
18.p: Lord, You gave us helpers and counselors. Make us humble enough to listen. Amen.
18.l: Ask someone for help today with something that is too big for you to do alone.
q: Moses was the greatest leader in Israel and still took advice. When do you find it hard to take advice?

19.o: This chapter introduces the solemnity of the giving of the law upon Mount Sinai, which was one of the most striking appearances of the divine glory that ever was in this lower world. We have here, I. The circumstances of time and place, ver. 1, 2. II. The covenant between God and Israel settled in general. The gracious proposal God made to them (ver. 3-6), and their consent to the proposal, ver. 7, 8. III. Notice given three days before of God's design to give the law out of a thick cloud, ver. 9.
19.i: Israel reaches Mount Sinai, where God invites them to be a holy nation and appears in fire and thunder.
19.p: Lord, You carried us on eagles' wings. Make us Your people, and help us to listen. Amen.
19.l: Listen for thunder or wind outside today, and remember that God is greater than the biggest storm.
q: Israel promised to obey before they knew all the commands. What would it mean for you to say yes to God first?

20.o: All things being prepared for the solemn promulgation of the divine law, we have, in this chapter, I. The ten commandments, as God himself spoke them upon Mount Sinai (ver. 1-17), as remarkable a portion of scripture as any in the Old Testament. II. The impressions made upon the people thereby, ver. 18-21. III. Some particular instructions which God gave privately to Moses, to be by him communicated to the people, relating to his worship, ver. 22, &c.
20.i: God speaks the Ten Commandments to Israel from Mount Sinai, and the people tremble at the thunder and the trumpet.
20.p: Lord, Your commandments are a gift. Write them on our hearts and help us to love You and others. Amen.
20.l: Pick one commandment today and think of a way to follow it.
q: God gave the commandments after He saved Israel, not before. Why does that order matter?

21.o: The laws recorded in this chapter relate to the fifth and sixth commandments; and though they are not accommodated to our constitution, especially in point of servitude, nor are the penalties annexed binding on us, yet they are of great use for the explanation of the moral law, and the rules of natural justice. Here are several enlargements, I. Upon the fifth commandment, which concerns particular relations. 1. The duty of masters towards their servants, their men-servants (ver. 2-6), and the maidservants, ver.
21.s: Laws for a People Who Had Been Slaves
21.i: Exodus 21 to 23 is the first collection of laws after the Ten Commandments, and it is full of the details of ordinary life.
21.p: Lord, You are a God of justice and mercy. Teach us to be fair, to care for strangers, and to protect those who cannot protect themselves. Amen.
21.l: Do one fair thing today that no one is making you do, like returning something you borrowed or sharing something you own.
q: Whose cause have you taken up lately?

22.o: The laws of this chapter relate, I. To the eighth commandment, concerning theft (ver. 1-4), trespass by cattle (ver. 5), damage by fire (ver. 6), trusts (ver. 7-13), borrowing cattle (ver. 14, 15), or money, ver. 25-27. II. To the seventh commandment. Against fornication (ver. 16, 17), bestiality, ver. 19. III. To the first table, forbidding witchcraft (ver. 18), idolatry, ver. 20. Commanding to offer the firstfruits, ver. 29, 30. IV. To the poor, ver. 21-24. V. To the civil government, ver. 28. VI.
22.s: Laws for a People Who Had Been Slaves
22.i: Exodus 21 to 23 is the first collection of laws after the Ten Commandments, and it is full of the details of ordinary life.
22.p: Lord, You are a God of justice and mercy. Teach us to be fair, to care for strangers, and to protect those who cannot protect themselves. Amen.
22.l: Do one fair thing today that no one is making you do, like returning something you borrowed or sharing something you own.
q: Whose cause have you taken up lately?

23.o: This chapter continues and concludes the acts that passed in the first session (if I may so call it) upon Mount Sinai. Here are, I. Some laws of universal obligation, relating especially to the ninth commandment, against bearing false witness (ver. 1), and giving false judgment, ver. 2, 3, 6-8. Also a law of doing good to our enemies (ver. 4, 5), and not oppressing strangers, ver. 9. II. Some laws peculiar to the Jews. The sabbatical year (ver. 10, 11), the three annual feasts (ver.
23.s: Laws for a People Who Had Been Slaves
23.i: Exodus 21 to 23 is the first collection of laws after the Ten Commandments, and it is full of the details of ordinary life.
23.p: Lord, You are a God of justice and mercy. Teach us to be fair, to care for strangers, and to protect those who cannot protect themselves. Amen.
23.l: Do one fair thing today that no one is making you do, like returning something you borrowed or sharing something you own.
q: Whose cause have you taken up lately?

24.o: Moses, as mediator between God and Israel, having received divers laws and ordinances from God privately in the three foregoing chapters, in this chapter, I. Comes down to the people, acquaints them with the laws he had received, and takes their consent to those laws (ver. 3), writes the laws, and reads them to the people, who repeat their consent (ver. 4-7), and then by sacrifice, and the sprinkling of blood, ratifies the covenant between them and God, ver. 5, 6, 8. II.
24.i: Israel promises twice to do all God says, Moses seals the covenant with blood, and the elders see God.
24.p: Lord, You made a covenant with us. Thank You for the blood of the covenant, and help us to keep our word. Amen.
24.l: Make a promise to God today in your own words, and ask Him to help you keep it.
q: Israel said yes twice before the blood was sprinkled. What do you need to say yes to?

25.o: At this chapter begins an account of the orders and instructions God gave to Moses upon the mount for the erecting and furnishing of a tabernacle to the honour of God. We have here. I. Orders given for a collection to be made among the people for this purpose, ver. 1-9. II. Particular instructions, 1. Concerning the ark of the covenant, ver. 10-22. 2. The table of showbread, ver. 23-30. 3. The golden candlestick, ver. 31, &c.
25.i: Exodus 25 to 27 describe a portable sanctuary with exact measurements, built so that God could live among a people on the move.
25.p: Lord, You chose to dwell among Your people. Make us a place where You are at home. Amen.
25.l: Make something with your hands today for someone else, and put care into every detail.
q: The ark held God's words, safe, in the middle of the camp. What do you keep at the center of your home or day?

26.o: Moses here receives instructions, I. Concerning the inner curtains of the tent or tabernacle, and the coupling of those curtains, ver. 1-6. II. Concerning the outer curtains which were of goats' hair, to strengthen the former, ver. 7-13. III. Concerning the case or cover which was to secure it from the weather, ver. 14. IV. Concerning the boards which were to be reared up to support the curtains, with their bars and sockets, ver. 15-30. V. The partition between the holy place and the most holy, ver. 31-35. VI.
26.i: Exodus 25 to 27 describe a portable sanctuary with exact measurements, built so that God could live among a people on the move.
26.p: Lord, You chose to dwell among Your people. Make us a place where You are at home. Amen.
26.l: Make something with your hands today for someone else, and put care into every detail.
q: The ark held God's words, safe, in the middle of the camp. What do you keep at the center of your home or day?

27.o: In this chapter directions are given, I. Concerning the brazen altar for burnt-offerings, ver. 1-8. II. Concerning the court of the tabernacle, with the hangings of it, ver. 9-19. III. Concerning oil for the lamp, ver. 20, 21.
27.i: Exodus 25 to 27 describe a portable sanctuary with exact measurements, built so that God could live among a people on the move.
27.p: Lord, You chose to dwell among Your people. Make us a place where You are at home. Amen.
27.l: Make something with your hands today for someone else, and put care into every detail.
q: The ark held God's words, safe, in the middle of the camp. What do you keep at the center of your home or day?

28.o: Orders being given for the fitting up of the place of worship, in this and the following chapter care is taken about the priests that were to minister in this holy place, as the menial servants of the God of Israel. He hired servants, as a token of his purpose to reside among them. In this chapter, I. He pitches upon the persons who should be his servants, ver. 1. II.
28.i: Exodus 28 and 29 describe the clothing and ordination of Israel's first priests, in which every detail carries a message.
28.p: Lord, You called priests to stand between You and Your people. Thank You for Jesus, our High Priest, who carries us. Amen.
28.l: Think of three people you care about and say a short prayer for each of them by name.
q: The garments were meant to remind priests of the dignity of the office. What do you wear, or carry, that reminds you who you are serving?

29.o: Particular orders are given in this chapter, I. Concerning the consecration of the priests, and the sanctification of the altar, ver. 1-37. II. Concerning the daily sacrifice, ver. 38-41. To which gracious promises are annexed that God would own and bless them in all their services, ver. 42, &c.
29.i: Exodus 28 and 29 describe the clothing and ordination of Israel's first priests, in which every detail carries a message.
29.p: Lord, You called priests to stand between You and Your people. Thank You for Jesus, our High Priest, who carries us. Amen.
29.l: Think of three people you care about and say a short prayer for each of them by name.
q: The garments were meant to remind priests of the dignity of the office. What do you wear, or carry, that reminds you who you are serving?

30.o: Moses is, in this chapter, further instructed, I. Concerning the altar of incense, ver. 1-10. II. Concerning the ransom-money which the Israelites were to pay, when they were numbered, ver. 11-16. III. Concerning the laver of brass, which was set for the priests to wash in, ver. 17-21. IV. Concerning the making up of the anointing oil, and the use of it, ver. 22-33. V. Concerning the incense and perfume which were to be burned on the golden altar, ver. 34, &c.
30.s: The Incense Altar and the Half-Shekel
30.i: Exodus 30 adds three more things to the tent: the altar of incense, the washing basin, and the half-shekel that every person gave.
30.p: Lord, let our prayers rise like incense, and teach us to treat rich and poor the same, as You do. Amen.
30.l: Say a short prayer at the start of your morning and at the end of your evening this week.
q: The altar had to be cleansed of the impurity the people's sins put on it. What in your own life needs a regular cleaning, not a one-time fix?

31.o: God is here drawing towards a conclusion of what he had to say to Moses upon the mount, where he had now been with him forty days and forty nights; and yet no more is recorded of what was said to him in all that time than what we have read in the six chapters foregoing. In this, I. He appoints what workmen should be employed in the building and furnishing of the tabernacle, ver. 1-11. II. He repeats the law of the sabbath, and the religious observance of it, ver. 12-17. III.
31.s: Filled with the Spirit to Make
31.i: God names Bezalel and Oholiab and fills them with His Spirit so they can build the tabernacle.
31.p: Lord, You are the giver of every skill. Teach us to use our hands for You. Amen.
31.l: Make something beautiful today, like a drawing or a song, and give it to someone as a gift.
q: God gave artists and builders His Spirit. How is your skill a gift from God?

32.o: It is a very lamentable interruption which the story of this chapter gives to the record of the establishment of the church, and of religion among the Jews. Things went on admirably well towards that happy settlement: God had shown himself very favourable, and the people also had seemed to be pretty tractable.
32.i: While Moses is on the mountain, the people ask Aaron for a god, and Moses pleads with God for them.
32.p: Lord, we turn away so easily. Forgive us, and bring us back to You. Amen.
32.l: Pray for someone who has made a bad choice, the way Moses did.
q: Moses stood between God and the people. Who is standing in the gap for you, and for whom do you stand?

33.o: In this chapter we have a further account of the mediation of Moses between God and Israel, for the making up of the breach that sin had made between them. I. He brings a very humbling message from God to them (ver. 1-3, 5), which has a good effect upon them, and helps to prepare them for mercy, ver. 4, 6. II.
33.s: Speaking with the Lord as a Friend
33.i: Moses meets God face to face in a tent outside the camp and asks to see His glory.
33.p: Lord, thank You that we may come to You. Show us Your goodness, and keep us in Your hand. Amen.
33.l: Find a quiet place today where you can talk to God like a friend, and tell Him what is on your mind.
q: Moses spoke to God as to a friend. What would it look like for you to talk with God that way?

34.o: God having in the foregoing chapter intimated to Moses his reconciliation to Israel, here gives proofs of it, proceeding to settle his covenant and communion with them. Four instances of the return of his favour we have in this chapter:—I. The orders he gives to Moses to come up to the mount, the next morning, and bring two tables of stone with him, ver. 1-4. II. His meeting him there, and the proclamation of his name, ver. 5-9. III.
34.i: After the calf, God renews the covenant, reveals His name to Moses, and Moses' face shines.
34.p: Lord, You are merciful and gracious. Change us as we spend time with You. Amen.
34.l: Spend a few quiet minutes with God today, then see whether it changes how you treat people.
q: Moses did not know his face was shining. Who has seen God in you without your noticing?

35.o: What should have been said and done upon Moses' coming down the first time from the mount, if the golden calf had not broken the measures and put all into disorder, now at last, when with great difficulty reconciliation was made, begins to be said and done; and that great affair of the setting up of God's worship is put into its former channel again, and goes on now without interruption. I. Moses gives Israel those instructions, received from God, which required immediate observance. 1. Concerning the sabbath, ver.
35.i: Exodus 35 to 39 tell how the tent was built: willing gifts, skilled hands, and a surprising moment when the leaders had to say stop.
35.p: Lord, we thank You for hearts that give gladly. Make us generous with what we have, and faithful with what You give us to do. Amen.
35.l: Give something today gladly, with no one asking you to, and notice how it feels.
q: No one thought anything too good to give to God. What have you kept back as too good?

36.o: In this chapter, I. The work of the tabernacle is begun, ver. 1-4. II. A stop is put to the people's contributions, ver. 5-7. III. A particular account is given of the making of the tabernacle itself; the fine curtains of it, ver. 8-13. The coarse ones, ver. 14-19. The boards, ver. 20-30. The bars, ver. 31-34. The partition veil, ver. 35, 36. And the hanging for the door, ver. 37, &c.
36.i: Exodus 35 to 39 tell how the tent was built: willing gifts, skilled hands, and a surprising moment when the leaders had to say stop.
36.p: Lord, we thank You for hearts that give gladly. Make us generous with what we have, and faithful with what You give us to do. Amen.
36.l: Give something today gladly, with no one asking you to, and notice how it feels.
q: No one thought anything too good to give to God. What have you kept back as too good?

37.o: Bezaleel and his workmen are still busy, making I. The ark with the mercy-seat and the cherubim, ver. 1-9. II. The table with its vessels, ver. 10-16. III. The candlestick with its appurtenances, ver. 17-24. IV. The golden altar for incense, ver. 25-28. V. The holy oil and incense, ver. 29. The particular appointment concerning each of which we had before the 25th and 30th chapters.
37.s: Bezalel Builds the Ark and the Lampstand
37.i: Exodus 37 is a builder's report: the furniture of the tabernacle, made one piece at a time, exactly as God showed Moses.
37.p: Lord, You made us to make good things with our hands. Give us skill and care in all we do for You. Amen.
37.l: Make something with your hands today and do your very best work on it, as if you were making it for God.
q: God's showings in this world are only candlelight. What light do you have, and do you trim it every morning?

38.o: Here is an account, I. Of the making of the brazen altar (ver. 1-7), and the laver, ver. 8. II. The preparing of the hangings for the enclosing of the court in which the tabernacle was to stand, ver. 9-20. III. A summary of the gold, silver, and brass, that was contributed to, and used in, the preparing of the tabernacle, ver. 21, &c.
38.i: Exodus 35 to 39 tell how the tent was built: willing gifts, skilled hands, and a surprising moment when the leaders had to say stop.
38.p: Lord, we thank You for hearts that give gladly. Make us generous with what we have, and faithful with what You give us to do. Amen.
38.l: Give something today gladly, with no one asking you to, and notice how it feels.
q: No one thought anything too good to give to God. What have you kept back as too good?

39.o: This chapter gives us an account of the finishing of the work of the tabernacle. I. The last things prepared were the holy garments. The ephod and its curious girdle, ver. 1-5. The onyx-stones for the shoulders, ver. 6, 7. The breastplate with the precious stones in it, ver. 8-21. The robe of the ephod, ver. 22-26. The coats, bonnets, and breeches, for the inferior priests, ver. 27-29. And the plate of the holy crown, ver. 30, 31. II.
39.i: Exodus 35 to 39 tell how the tent was built: willing gifts, skilled hands, and a surprising moment when the leaders had to say stop.
39.p: Lord, we thank You for hearts that give gladly. Make us generous with what we have, and faithful with what You give us to do. Amen.
39.l: Give something today gladly, with no one asking you to, and notice how it feels.
q: No one thought anything too good to give to God. What have you kept back as too good?

40.o: In this chapter, I. Orders are given for the setting up of the tabernacle and the fixing of all the appurtenances of it in their proper places (ver. 1-8), and the consecrating of it (ver. 9-11), and of the priests, ver. 12-15. II. Care is taken to do all this, and as it was appointed to be done, ver. 16-33. III. God takes possession of it by the cloud, ver. 34, &c.
40.i: Moses sets up the tabernacle exactly as God commanded, and God's glory fills it.
40.p: Lord, thank You for dwelling among us. Make our hearts a home for You. Amen.
40.l: Make a spot in your home today for prayer, and spend a few minutes there.
q: God lived in a tent among His people. What does that tell you about how close He wants to be?
